intro: Bible study means reading a passage slowly, understanding it with the Church, praying with it, and letting it change one thing in your week. Start with the short guide, then follow a plan.
prayer: Come, Holy Spirit. Open my heart to your Word. Help me hear what you want to say to me today, and give me the grace to live it. Amen.

method.name: Read
method.about: Read the passage slowly, twice if you can. Reading it aloud helps. Notice a word or line that stands out.

method.name: Understand
method.about: Ask what it meant when it was written. A short note helps you, with a Catechism paragraph to go further.

method.name: Pray
method.about: Use the questions to talk with God about what struck you. Write a line or two if you like.

method.name: Live
method.about: Choose one small step for this week. God's Word is meant to be lived, not only read.

guide.title: The Bible is a library
body: The Bible is not one book but a library of 73 books, written over more than a thousand years by many writers. The Church teaches that God is its true author: he inspired the human writers, who wrote in their own words and styles (Catechism 105-106).

The Old Testament has 46 books: the story of God and his people Israel, the prophets, and prayers like the Psalms. The New Testament has 27 books: the four Gospels about Jesus, the Acts of the Apostles, letters to the first Christians, and Revelation.
Catholic Bibles have seven books that most Protestant Bibles leave out, such as Tobit, Wisdom and 1 and 2 Maccabees. That is why a Catholic Bible is a little thicker.

guide.title: How to find a passage
body: A reference like Luke 24:13-35 means: the book of Luke, chapter 24, verses 13 to 35. The big number is the chapter, the small numbers after the colon are the verses.
Use the table of contents at the front. The four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) open the New Testament, about three quarters of the way through.
You will see short names too: Mt, Mk, Lk and Jn for the Gospels, Gn for Genesis, Ps for Psalms, 1 Cor for the First Letter to the Corinthians.

One small surprise: older Catholic Bibles, like the Douay-Rheims used in this app, number most Psalms one lower. The Psalm "The Lord is my shepherd" is Psalm 23 in a modern Bible. In the Douay-Rheims it is Psalm 22 and begins "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing."

guide.title: Which Bible to use in Canada
body: At Mass in Canada, the readings come from the Lectionary approved by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. It is based on the New Revised Standard Version (NRSV).

For your own Bible, choose a Catholic edition with all 73 books. The NRSV Catholic Edition matches the wording you hear at Mass in Canada. The Revised Standard Version, Second Catholic Edition, is another good choice. Look for "Catholic Edition" on the cover.

Inside Heartward, the passages are from the Douay-Rheims, an older Catholic translation that anyone may share freely. That lets the app keep the text on your phone, so it works offline. Its English is old fashioned: "thee" means you, and "charity" means love. Each study also links to the passage in the NRSV.

guide.title: How Catholics read the Bible
body: Catholics read the Bible with the Church, not alone. Scripture and Tradition come from the same source, God, and they belong together (Catechism 80-82).

The Catechism gives three simple rules: read each passage as part of the whole Bible, read it within the living Tradition of the Church, and read it in harmony with the faith as a whole (Catechism 112-114).
A passage has a literal sense, what the writer meant to say, and a spiritual sense, how it points to Christ, to how we should live, and to heaven (Catechism 115-117).
If a passage is hard or troubling, that is normal. Write your question down and bring it to your catechist, your sponsor or a priest.

guide.title: Where to start
body: Start with the Gospels, because they are about Jesus himself. Mark is the shortest and moves quickly. Luke shows God's mercy again and again.
Read this Sunday's Gospel before Mass. You will hear it with new ears.
The Psalms are prayers you can borrow when you do not have your own words.

guide.title: Making it a habit
body: Ten or fifteen minutes is enough. Keep the same time and place each day if you can, like morning coffee or before bed.
Begin with a short prayer to the Holy Spirit. Read slowly. Write one line about what struck you. End with an Our Father.
Missing a day is fine. Just pick up where you left off.

s01.understand: Two disciples leave Jerusalem on Easter Sunday, sad and confused. Jesus joins them, explains the Scriptures, and they recognize him when he breaks bread. The Church sees the shape of the Mass here: first the Word, then the Eucharist.
s01.live: Take a slow walk this week and talk to Jesus as if he were walking beside you.

s03.understand: Jesus warns against praying to be seen and gives his disciples the Our Father. The Church calls it the summary of the whole Gospel: it teaches us what to ask for and in what order.
s03.live: Pray the Our Father slowly once a day, stopping after each line.

sym1-01.understand: Before he returns to the Father, Jesus sends the apostles to all nations. He tells them to baptize in one name, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: one God in three Persons. He promises to stay with us always.
sym1-01.live: Make the Sign of the Cross slowly each morning, remembering that it names the Trinity.

sym1-02.understand: The religious leaders complain that Jesus eats with sinners. He answers with two stories about searching. God is the one who goes looking, and heaven rejoices over one person who comes home.
sym1-02.live: Thank God for one way he came looking for you on your journey to the Church.

sym1-03.understand: Paul, near the end of his life, reminds Timothy that Scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching and for growing in holiness. The Church teaches that God speaks to us through human words.
sym1-03.live: Choose a regular time this week to read the Bible for ten minutes.

sym1-04.understand: The serpent plants doubt, and the first humans stop trusting God. Their sin wounds everything. But in the same chapter, God promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent. The Church calls this the first announcement of the Gospel.
sym1-04.live: Notice one moment this week when you are tempted to doubt God's goodness, and say a short prayer of trust.

sym1-05.understand: Jesus asks his friends who they say he is. Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom, and the Church sees here the beginning of Peter's role among the apostles.
sym1-05.live: Answer Jesus' question in your own words, and write it down.

sym1-06.understand: John tells the crucifixion simply. Jesus carries his cross, gives his mother to the beloved disciple, and says "It is consummated" (in modern Bibles, "It is finished"): his work of love is complete. He gives his life freely for us.
sym1-06.live: Look at a crucifix for one quiet minute each day and say thank you.

sym1-07.understand: Fifty days after Easter, the Holy Spirit comes on the disciples gathered in prayer, like wind and fire. They speak so that people of every nation understand. This is the birthday of the Church.
sym1-07.live: Before each meal or task this week, pray: "Come, Holy Spirit."

sym1-08.understand: The first Christians held to four things: the apostles' teaching, the community, the breaking of bread, and the prayers. The Church still lives these today, especially at Sunday Mass.
sym1-08.live: Introduce yourself to one person at your parish this week.

sym1-09.understand: The angel Gabriel greets Mary as full of grace and asks her to become the mother of the Son of God. She asks how, then gives her free yes: "be it done to me according to thy word."
sym1-09.live: Pray the Hail Mary each day, thinking of Mary's yes.

sym1-10.understand: Jesus weeps at the tomb of his friend, then calls Lazarus out alive. He tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life." Our hope in eternal life rests on Jesus himself.
sym1-10.live: Pray for someone you love who has died, and for those who mourn them.

sym2-01.understand: Nicodemus, a teacher, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him he must be "born again of water and the Holy Ghost" (the Holy Spirit). The Church understands this as Baptism, the door to new life.
sym2-01.live: Bless yourself with holy water when you enter church, remembering Baptism.

sym2-02.understand: Jesus says he is the bread of life and that his flesh is real food. Many disciples find this too hard and leave. Peter stays: "Lord, to whom shall we go?" The Church sees here Jesus' promise of the Eucharist.
sym2-02.live: At Mass this week, watch the moment the priest lifts the Host, and say quietly, "My Lord and my God."

sym2-03.understand: At the Passover meal, Jesus takes bread and says, "This is my body." Over the cup he speaks of "the new testament in my blood" (testament means covenant). He tells the apostles to do this in memory of him. Every Mass makes this gift present.
sym2-03.live: Listen closely for these words of Jesus at the next Mass you attend.

sym2-04.understand: A son wastes everything and comes home ashamed. His father runs to meet him before he can finish his apology. This is the picture of God's mercy in the sacrament of Confession.
sym2-04.live: Say an Act of Contrition each night, trusting the Father runs to meet you.

sym2-05.understand: At a wedding, the wine runs out. Mary tells the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Jesus' first sign is at a marriage, and the Church sees in it his blessing on marriage.
sym2-05.live: Pray for a married couple you know, and for anyone you know preparing for marriage or priesthood.

sym2-06.understand: Jesus begins his Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes. They describe what the happiness of God's kingdom looks like, and they paint a portrait of Jesus himself.
sym2-06.live: Pick one Beatitude and look for a chance to live it this week.

sym2-07.understand: Paul writes to a quarrelsome church that gifts and knowledge mean nothing without love. Love, which the Douay-Rheims calls charity, is patient and kind and never ends. It is the greatest of the virtues.
sym2-07.live: Read verses 4 to 7 again and put your name in place of "charity." Where is God inviting you to grow?

sym2-08.understand: God sees that it is not good for the man to be alone and creates the woman. They are equal, made for each other, and become "one flesh." Jesus points back to this passage when he speaks of marriage.
sym2-08.live: Thank God for the people he has given you so that you are not alone.

sym2-09.understand: Jesus describes the last judgment. What we do for the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner, we do for him. The Church lists these as the works of mercy.
sym2-09.live: Do one work of mercy this week: a meal, a visit, a donation or a kind call.

sym2-10.understand: God creates man and woman in his own image and blesses them, and he sees everything he made as very good. Every person, without exception, carries this dignity.
sym2-10.live: When someone annoys you this week, remind yourself silently: "made in God's image."

s26.understand: Jesus speaks about three practices: giving to the poor, praying, and fasting. Do them for God, not to be seen. The Church makes these the three pillars of Lent.
s26.live: Choose one small act of prayer, fasting and almsgiving for this week.

s27.understand: Jesus gives sight to a man born blind. The man's faith grows step by step, while others refuse to see. Early Christians called Baptism "enlightenment," and this Gospel is read at the scrutinies during Lent.
s27.live: Ask Jesus to show you one thing in your life you have not wanted to see.

s28.understand: Paul hands on what he received: Christ died for our sins, was buried, rose on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses. This is the heart of the Creed you will soon profess.
s28.live: Pray the Creed slowly once this week, and stop at the line that moves you most.

s29.understand: The disciples ask Jesus to teach them to pray, and he gives them the Our Father. Then he tells of a friend who knocks at midnight: keep asking, because the Father loves to give the Holy Spirit.
s29.live: Bring one need to God every day this week, and don't give up.

s30.understand: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty and weeps. Jesus calls her by name, and she knows him. He sends her to tell the apostles. She is the first witness of the Resurrection.
s30.live: Tell one person this week why Easter matters to you.

s31.understand: This passage returns to the first Christians: teaching, community, the breaking of bread and prayer. Now that you have received the sacraments, this is the life you share with them.
s31.live: Choose one way to keep growing after Easter: a parish group, a ministry, or daily prayer.

s32.understand: The road began here and ends here. After the two disciples recognize Jesus, they get up at once and run back to tell the others. Every Mass ends the same way: go and announce the Gospel.
s32.live: Share your story of coming to the Church with one person this week.

s02.understand: John does not say only that God loves; he says God is love. From all eternity the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit live in an exchange of love, and God made us to share in it. We did not earn this love or start it: God loved us first and sent his Son to take away our sins. Whoever lives in love lives in God.
s02.live: Each night this week, name one way God showed you his love that day.

rcia.title: My RCIA road
rcia.sub: One passage for each session, in order
rcia.about: Each week of RCIA has a Bible passage that goes with the lesson. Study it before or after class. The one for your next session is marked.

mark.title: Meet Jesus in Mark
mark.about: Mark is the shortest Gospel and the best place to start. One chapter a day takes you through the whole life of Jesus in about two weeks. Mark writes quickly: watch for the word "immediately."

days.title: The beginning
days.intro: John the Baptist prepares the way, Jesus is baptized, calls the first disciples and heals many.
days.understand: Mark starts with no Christmas story: he jumps straight to Jesus' public life. At his baptism the Father speaks and the Spirit descends, so the whole Trinity is present. Jesus then calls ordinary fishermen to follow him.
questions: Simon and Andrew left their nets "immediately." What is one net you find hard to leave?
Jesus gets up early to pray alone (verse 35). When could you do the same?
days.live: Find a quiet five minutes early in the day to pray, as Jesus did.

days.title: Who can forgive sins?
days.intro: Friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof, Jesus forgives his sins, calls a tax collector and eats with sinners.
days.understand: Jesus first says "thy sins are forgiven," and the scribes are shocked, because only God can forgive sins. Healing the man shows he has that power. Jesus gave this power to his apostles, and it lives on in Confession.
questions: The friends carried the man to Jesus. Who carried you toward Jesus?
Who could you carry to Jesus in prayer this week?
days.live: Pray by name for one friend who needs Jesus.

days.title: Jesus chooses the Twelve
days.intro: Crowds come from everywhere. Jesus chooses twelve apostles and says who his true family is.
days.understand: Jesus goes up a mountain and chooses twelve, like the twelve tribes of Israel: he is gathering a new People of God. The Church is built on these apostles, and the bishops are their successors.
questions: Jesus called "whom he would himself" (verse 13). How does it feel to know you are chosen?
Jesus says whoever does God's will is his brother, sister and mother. What does that mean for you?
days.live: Learn the name of your bishop and pray for him.

days.title: Seeds and storms
days.intro: The parable of the sower, the mustard seed, and Jesus calming the storm.
days.understand: Parables are short stories that invite us to think. The seed is God's Word, and we are the soil. In the storm, the disciples learn that Jesus is Lord even of wind and sea.
questions: Which kind of soil are you most like right now?
What storm in your life do you need to bring to Jesus?
days.live: When you feel worried this week, pray the words of Jesus: "Peace, be still."

days.title: Power over evil, sickness and death
days.intro: Jesus frees a man from many demons, heals a woman who touches his cloak, and raises a little girl.
days.understand: Three stories show Jesus' power over everything that harms us. The woman had suffered twelve years and the girl was twelve years old. To both, Jesus says that faith is what opens the door.
questions: The woman only touched his cloak. What does it mean to reach out to Jesus in faith?
Jesus tells Jairus, "Fear not, only believe." Where do you need to hear that?
days.live: Bring one fear to Jesus each day this week and leave it with him.

days.title: Bread in the desert
days.intro: Jesus is rejected at home, sends out the Twelve, feeds five thousand and walks on the water.
days.understand: Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it: the same four actions as at the Last Supper and at every Mass. The miracle points ahead to the Eucharist.
questions: The disciples had only five loaves and two fish. What small thing could you offer Jesus?
Even at home, people doubted Jesus. Have you faced doubt from people close to you?
days.live: At Mass, watch for the four actions: take, bless, break, give.

days.title: A clean heart
days.intro: What truly makes a person unclean, a mother's faith, and the healing of a deaf man.
days.understand: Jesus teaches that evil comes from the heart, not from food. He heals a deaf man by touching him and saying "Ephpheta": be thou opened. The priest uses this gesture at some Baptisms, praying that we hear God's Word.
questions: The mother kept asking even when it was hard. What do you keep asking God for?
What would you like Jesus to "open" in you?
days.live: Before reading the Bible, touch your ears and pray, "Lord, open my ears to your Word."

days.title: Who do you say I am?
days.intro: Another feeding, Peter's answer, and the first time Jesus speaks of the cross.
days.understand: This is the turning point of Mark. Peter says Jesus is the Christ, but cannot accept a suffering Messiah. Jesus says that to follow him means to take up our own cross.
questions: Who do you say Jesus is today?
What cross is in front of you right now?
days.live: Offer one difficult moment this week to Jesus, joined to his cross.

days.title: On the mountain
days.intro: The Transfiguration, the healing of a boy, and an argument about who is the greatest.
days.understand: On the mountain the apostles see Jesus' glory, to strengthen them for the cross ahead. Then a father cries, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." It is a prayer anyone can pray.
questions: Have you had a "mountain" moment when God felt close?
Is "help my unbelief" a prayer you need?
days.live: Pray "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief" whenever doubts come this week.

days.title: The way of the servant
days.intro: Marriage, little children, a rich man who walks away, and blind Bartimaeus who follows.
days.understand: Jesus teaches that marriage is for life, welcomes children, and invites a rich man to leave everything. He says he came "not to be ministered unto, but to minister." Bartimaeus, healed, follows Jesus on the road.
questions: Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him. What might Jesus ask you to let go of?
Bartimaeus kept calling out. What would you shout to Jesus?
days.live: Do one quiet act of service this week that nobody will notice.

days.title: The King arrives
days.intro: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt, clears the Temple, and teaches about faith and forgiveness.
days.understand: The crowd cries "Hosanna," the words we sing at every Mass before the Eucharistic Prayer. Jesus is a humble king who comes on a colt, not a war horse. On Palm Sunday the Church walks this road with him.
questions: How do you welcome Jesus into your life?
Jesus links prayer and forgiveness (verse 25). Who do you need to forgive?
days.live: Sing or say the Holy, Holy ("Hosanna in the highest") with attention at your next Mass.

days.title: The greatest commandment
days.intro: Questions in the Temple, the two great commandments, and a poor widow's gift.
days.understand: Asked for the first commandment, Jesus joins two: love God with all you are, and love your neighbour as yourself. The poor widow gives only two small coins, but she gives everything.
questions: Which is harder for you: loving God with all your heart, or loving your neighbour?
What would it mean to give God "all" like the widow?
days.live: Give something this week that costs you a little: time, money or patience.

days.title: Stay awake
days.intro: Jesus speaks of the end of the age and tells his friends to watch.
days.understand: Jesus warns of hard times but tells his disciples not to be afraid. No one knows the day or hour of his return, so the point is not to guess but to be ready, living each day faithfully.
questions: Jesus says "Watch" three times. What does being watchful look like in daily life?
What would you want to be doing when Jesus comes?
days.live: End each day this week by asking: did I live today ready to meet Jesus?

days.title: The night before
days.intro: A woman anoints Jesus, the Last Supper, the prayer in Gethsemane, his arrest, and Peter's denial.
days.understand: At supper Jesus gives his Body and Blood. In the garden he prays "Abba, Father" and accepts the Father's will. Peter, who promised never to leave, denies him three times, then weeps.
questions: Jesus asks his friends to stay awake with him. How can you keep him company?
Peter failed and wept. How does his story give you hope?
days.live: Spend a few minutes with Jesus in a church or chapel this week, keeping him company.

days.title: The cross
days.intro: Jesus before Pilate, the crucifixion, his death and burial.
days.understand: Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22, a prayer that begins in anguish and ends in trust. When he dies, a Roman soldier says, "Indeed this man was the son of God." The first to confess this is a stranger.
questions: Simon of Cyrene helped carry the cross. Whose cross could you help carry?
What does the centurion's words mean to you?
days.live: Help someone with a burden this week, like Simon of Cyrene.

days.title: He is risen
days.intro: The women find the tomb empty. The risen Jesus appears and sends the disciples into the whole world.
days.understand: The women come to anoint a body and find an angel instead: "He is risen, he is not here." Jesus sends the disciples to preach to every creature. The story continues in us.
questions: The women were afraid at first. What makes the Resurrection hard or wonderful to believe?
Who in your life needs good news?
days.live: Thank God for walking you through the whole Gospel, and choose the next Gospel to read.

story.title: The big story
story.sub: 15 moments from Creation to the new creation
story.about: The Bible tells one story: God makes us, we turn away, and God never stops coming after us until he sends his Son. These fifteen moments give you the whole map, so every passage you hear at Mass has a place.

days.title: Creation
days.intro: God makes everything, and makes man and woman in his image.
days.understand: Genesis tells the truth that God made everything out of love, and that it is good. It is not a science textbook; it answers who made the world and why. Human beings are the crown of creation.
questions: God sees that it is "very good." What in creation fills you with wonder?
What does it mean to you to be made in God's image?
days.live: Step outside once this week just to look at creation and thank God.

days.title: The fall
days.intro: The first sin, and the first promise of a Savior.
days.understand: Adam and Eve stop trusting God and choose their own way. Sin brings shame, blame and death. But God goes looking: "Where art thou?" and promises that evil will be crushed.
questions: God asks Adam, "Where art thou?" How would you answer today?
Why do you think they hid from God?
days.live: When you notice yourself hiding from God this week, turn back with a short prayer.

days.title: Noah and the rainbow
days.intro: After the flood, God makes a covenant with all living things.
days.understand: A covenant is a sacred family bond, stronger than a contract. God promises Noah he will never destroy the earth by flood, and gives the rainbow as a sign. The Church sees the flood as a picture of Baptism.
questions: What promises of God do you hold on to?
What does a rainbow remind you of now?
days.live: Each time you see water this week, remember your Baptism (or the one you are preparing for).

days.title: Abraham's journey
days.intro: God calls Abram to leave home and promises to bless all nations through him.
days.understand: Abraham trusts God and sets out without knowing where he is going. He is our father in faith. God's promise to bless all nations through him comes true in Jesus.
questions: Like Abraham, you are on a journey. What have you had to leave behind?
What makes it hard to trust God with the unknown?
days.live: Hand one uncertain thing to God each morning this week.

days.title: The burning bush
days.intro: God calls Moses and tells him his name.
days.understand: God hears his people's cry in slavery and comes to save them. He tells Moses his name, "I am who am": God simply is, and is always with us. Jews do not say this name out of reverence.
questions: God says, "I have seen the affliction of my people." Do you believe God sees what you carry?
Moses took off his shoes. Where is your holy ground?
days.live: Make a small sign of reverence when you enter church: a bow or a genuflection, done slowly.

days.title: The Passover
days.intro: The lamb's blood on the doors, and the night of freedom.
days.understand: Each family sacrifices a lamb and eats it, and its blood saves them. The Jewish people still remember this every year. Jesus is the new Passover Lamb, and the Mass is the new Passover meal.
questions: At Mass the priest says "Behold the Lamb of God." What does that mean to you now?
What has God freed you from?
days.live: Listen for "Lamb of God" at Mass this week and remember the Passover.

days.title: The Ten Commandments
days.intro: God gives his people the ten words of the covenant.
days.understand: God first frees his people, then gives them the commandments. They are a way to stay free, not a burden. The first three are about loving God, the other seven about loving our neighbour.
questions: Which commandment do you find most freeing? Which is hardest?
Why do you think God gave the commandments after freeing his people, not before?
days.live: Use the commandments as a short examination of conscience one night this week.

days.title: A king forever
days.intro: God promises King David a son whose kingdom will last forever.
days.understand: David wants to build God a house, but God promises to build David a "house," a royal family. His throne will be firm forever. The angel tells Mary that Jesus will receive the throne of David.
questions: God says, "I took thee out of the pastures." Where did God find you?
How is Jesus a king unlike any other?
days.live: Pray "Thy kingdom come" slowly each day this week.

days.title: A new covenant
days.intro: In a time of exile, God promises to write his law on our hearts.
days.understand: The people broke the covenant and lost their land. Yet through the prophets God promises something new: a covenant written on hearts, with sins forgiven. At the Last Supper Jesus speaks of "the new testament in my blood": the new covenant has come.
questions: What would it mean to have God's law written on your heart?
God says "I will remember their sin no more." How does that feel?
days.live: Ask God each morning to write his love on your heart.

days.title: The suffering servant
days.intro: A servant who carries the sins of many.
days.understand: Hundreds of years before Jesus, Isaiah describes a servant despised, wounded for our sins, and silent like a lamb. The first Christians saw Jesus in these words, and the Church reads them on Good Friday.
questions: "By his bruises we are healed." What needs healing in you?
Which line describes Jesus most clearly to you?
days.live: Pray for someone who is suffering unjustly.

days.title: God is born
days.intro: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, and shepherds come to see.
days.understand: The promised King is born in a stable, laid in a manger, and announced first to poor shepherds. God became one of us. This is the Incarnation.
questions: Why do you think God chose such a humble beginning?
Mary kept these things in her heart. What do you keep in yours?
days.live: Place a nativity or a picture of the Holy Family where you will see it, whatever the season.

days.title: The cross
days.intro: Jesus is crucified between two thieves and forgives.
days.understand: On the cross Jesus forgives those who crucify him and promises paradise to a thief who asks. His death is the sacrifice of the new covenant, the Lamb given for the world.
questions: "Lord, remember me." Can you pray the thief's prayer?
Jesus forgives even here. Who is hardest for you to forgive?
days.live: Pray "Jesus, remember me" each night this week.

days.title: He is risen
days.intro: The women find the tomb empty on the first day of the week.
days.understand: "Why seek you the living with the dead?" The Resurrection is the centre of our faith. Sunday is the Lord's Day because Jesus rose on the first day of the week.
questions: The apostles first thought the women's words were nonsense. What helps you believe?
How can you make Sunday different from the other days?
days.live: Make this Sunday a true Lord's Day: Mass, rest and time with people you love.

days.title: The Church is born
days.intro: At Pentecost Peter preaches and three thousand are baptized.
days.understand: Filled with the Spirit, Peter announces Jesus. The people ask, "What shall we do?" He answers: repent and be baptized. The story of God's people continues in the Church.
questions: The crowd "had compunction in their heart": they were deeply moved. Have you felt that?
Peter's answer is for you too. What is your next step?
days.live: Talk with your sponsor or catechist about your next step toward the sacraments.

days.title: All things new
days.intro: A new heaven and a new earth, where God wipes away every tear.
days.understand: The Bible ends where it began, with God making something new. God will live with his people, and there will be no more death or mourning. This is the hope that carries us.
questions: Which tear would you most like God to wipe away?
How does this hope change the way you live today?
days.live: Tell someone who is grieving that you are praying for them.

free.title: Living free in Christ
free.sub: 7 studies on the freedom Jesus gives
free.about: Jesus came to set us free: from sin, from fear, from shame and from ourselves. These studies show that Christian freedom is not doing whatever we want, but becoming who God made us to be. The study on surrendering to God, with the Surrender Novena, is the heart of the series.

days.title: The truth will set you free
days.intro: Jesus tells those who believe in him that the truth will make them free, and that whoever sins is a slave.
days.understand: His listeners are offended: they say they have never been slaves. Jesus points to a deeper slavery, the one inside us, where sin keeps us from doing the good we want. Only the Son can free us, because he is the truth in person. Freedom begins when we stay in his word.
questions: What habit or fear makes you feel less than free?
Jesus says freedom comes from "remaining" in his word. What would that look like in your day?
Where have you already tasted the freedom Jesus gives?
days.live: Each evening this week, name one moment when you chose what was good, and thank Jesus for that freedom.

days.title: Surrender to God: the freedom of letting go
days.intro: James asks where our fights come from, and gives the answer: submit to God, resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Some study guides call this lesson "Finding Freedom through Submission."
days.understand: To submit sounds like losing freedom. James shows the opposite. Quarrels, envy and restlessness come from desires that rule us. When we hand ourselves over to God, who loves us, we stop being pushed around by those desires, and the devil loses his grip. The Church teaches that the more we do what is good, the freer we become, while choosing evil leads to slavery. Mary is the model: her "let it be done to me" made her the freest of all creatures. Submission here is not to a tyrant but to a Father, and it is always a free choice: "Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you." The Surrender Novena of Fr. Dolindo Ruotolo puts it in one line: "O Jesus, I surrender myself to you, take care of everything!"
questions: James says our conflicts come from desires at war within us. Which desire tends to rule you?
What is the difference between giving in to a person who controls you and giving yourself to God who loves you?
Is there one area of your life you are holding back from God? What might change if you let it go?
days.live: Pray Mary's words each morning this week: "Be it done to me according to your word," and hand God one worry or plan for that day.

days.title: Free from fear
days.intro: In the storm at night, Jesus walks on the water and calls Peter to come to him.
days.understand: The disciples are alone, tired and afraid. Jesus comes to them in the middle of the storm, not after it. Peter walks on the water while he looks at Jesus, and sinks when he looks at the wind. Even then, one short prayer, "Lord, save me," is enough: Jesus reaches out at once. Faith is a gift we keep alive by turning our eyes back to him.
questions: What "storm" are you in right now?
What makes you take your eyes off Jesus?
Peter's prayer is three words long. What short prayer could you keep ready for frightening moments?
days.live: Choose a short prayer, like "Jesus, I trust in you," and say it every time you feel afraid this week.

days.title: Free to love
days.intro: Paul tells the Galatians they were called to freedom, but not freedom to please themselves: freedom to serve one another in love.
days.understand: Paul sets two ways of living side by side: the works of the flesh, which divide and destroy, and the fruit of the Spirit, which grows by itself when we stay close to God. The Church calls the Gospel a law of freedom, because it moves us from the inside by love rather than by fear. Freedom is for love.
questions: Which fruit of the Spirit do you most want to grow in?
Paul says freedom can become an excuse. Where might you use freedom as an excuse?
Who could you serve in love this week?
days.live: Do one hidden act of service this week for someone who cannot repay you.

days.title: Forgiven much, free to love much
days.intro: A woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears at a Pharisee's dinner.
days.understand: Simon the Pharisee sees only her past. Jesus sees her love, and her love shows she knows she has been forgiven. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus does it here by his own word: "Your sins are forgiven. Go in peace." Shame tells us to hide; Jesus calls us out of hiding and sends us away free.
questions: Do you identify more with Simon or with the woman? Why?
Is there something in your past you still carry with shame?
What does Jesus' word "Go in peace" mean to you?
days.live: Bring one thing you are ashamed of to Jesus in prayer, and if you are baptized, plan to bring it to Confession.

days.title: Free from anxiety
days.intro: From prison, Paul writes: rejoice always, do not worry about anything, and bring everything to God in prayer.
days.understand: Paul is not writing from a comfortable life; he is in chains. Still he speaks of a peace beyond understanding that guards the heart. His secret is simple: turn every worry into a prayer, with thanksgiving, and fill the mind with what is true, good and beautiful. Every need can become a prayer.
questions: What are you most anxious about this week?
Paul adds "with thanksgiving." What can you thank God for even now?
What do you fill your mind with? What could you change?
days.live: Each time you notice a worry this week, turn it into a one-line prayer, and add one thank you.

days.title: Strong in the Lord
days.intro: Paul tells Christians to put on the armour of God, because our struggle is a spiritual one.
days.understand: Freedom has to be defended. Paul is honest that there is a real battle against evil, and the Church teaches the same. But we do not fight alone or with our own strength: truth, justice, the Gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God are all gifts. The last weapon is prayer, at all times, in the Spirit.
questions: Which piece of the armour do you most need right now?
Where do you feel the spiritual struggle in your life?
How can the word of God be a "sword" for you this week?
days.live: Learn one short verse by heart this week to pray when you are tempted.

praying.title: Learning to pray
praying.sub: 7 studies on how Jesus prays and teaches us to pray
praying.about: The disciples watched Jesus pray and asked him to teach them. These passages show how Jesus prays, what he says about prayer, and how the first Christians kept praying. Pray before you read, and let each study end in a few quiet minutes with God.

days.title: Jesus goes off to pray
days.intro: After a long day of healing, Jesus rises before dawn and goes to a lonely place to pray.
days.understand: Everyone is looking for Jesus, yet he makes time to be alone with his Father. His mission flows from that prayer: right after it, he goes on to the next towns. If Jesus needed quiet time with the Father, so do we. Prayer is not one more task; it is where the day finds its direction.
questions: When and where could you find a quiet place to pray?
What usually crowds out your prayer?
How might your day change if it began with God?
days.live: Before you look at your phone each morning this week, spend two minutes in silence with God.

days.title: Ask, seek, knock
days.intro: Jesus promises that whoever asks receives, and compares God to a father who gives good things to his children.
days.understand: Jesus wants us to ask boldly and keep asking. He reasons from ordinary life: no loving parent gives a child a stone instead of bread. How much more will the Father give good things to those who ask. Sometimes his answer is different from what we expected, but it is always a gift from a Father.
questions: Is it easy or hard for you to ask God for things? Why?
What do you want to ask God for today?
Can you remember a time God answered in a way you did not expect?
days.live: Write down one request each day this week, and look back at the list at the end of the week.

days.title: The widow who would not give up
days.intro: Jesus tells a parable about a widow who keeps coming to an unjust judge until he gives her justice.
days.understand: Luke tells us the point before the story: we should always pray and not lose heart. If even a careless judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who loves us, listen. The question at the end is for us: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith? Persistent prayer is faith that keeps knocking.
questions: Is there a prayer you have stopped praying because nothing seemed to happen?
What helps you keep praying when you feel discouraged?
What does it mean to you that God is not like the unjust judge?
days.live: Pick up one prayer you had given up on, and pray it every day this week.

days.title: The Pharisee and the tax collector
days.intro: Two men go up to the Temple to pray. One boasts; the other only says, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner."
days.understand: The Pharisee's prayer is really about himself. The tax collector stands far off and tells the truth about his need, and he goes home made right with God. The Church teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer. His short prayer became the Jesus Prayer, prayed by Christians for centuries.
questions: Do you ever compare yourself with others when you pray?
What would it mean to tell God the plain truth about yourself?
Try praying the tax collector's words slowly. What do you notice?
days.live: Pray "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner" ten times slowly each day this week.

days.title: Not my will, but yours
days.intro: In Gethsemane, the night before he dies, Jesus prays in anguish and gives himself to the Father's will.
days.understand: Jesus does not hide his feelings: he is deeply troubled and asks that the cup pass from him. He calls God "Abba," Father, and then says the hardest words of all: not what I will, but what you will. The disciples sleep, and he gently tells them to watch and pray. Honest prayer and trusting surrender belong together.
questions: Have you ever told God honestly that you did not want what was happening?
What makes "your will be done" hard to pray?
Jesus asks his friends to stay awake with him. How can you keep him company?
days.live: This week, end each prayer with the words "Not my will, but yours be done."

days.title: Pray without ceasing
days.intro: Paul gives the young Church three short commands: rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks in all circumstances.
days.understand: Praying without ceasing does not mean saying words all day. It means living the whole day with God: turning to him often, offering our work, thanking him in small moments. The Church says prayer and Christian life cannot be separated. Paul ends with a promise: the God who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.
questions: What small moments in your day could become moments of prayer?
Is it possible to give thanks in all circumstances? What helps?
What does "he who calls you is faithful" mean for you today?
days.live: Pick three daily moments, like waking, eating and going to bed, and say a short prayer at each one.

days.title: The Lord is my shepherd
days.intro: The best-loved psalm: God as a shepherd who leads, feeds, protects and stays with us even in the dark valley.
days.understand: The psalms are the prayer book of Jesus and of the Church, and Catholics pray them every day in the Liturgy of the Hours. Psalm 23 moves from green pastures to the darkest valley to a feast, and in every place the Lord is there. Jesus calls himself the Good Shepherd. In older Catholic Bibles, like the Douay-Rheims shown here, this psalm is numbered 22.
questions: Which line of the psalm speaks to you most today?
Where is your "dark valley" right now? What does it mean that God is with you there?
How has God "restored your soul" on your journey?
days.live: Learn Psalm 23 by heart this week, a line or two each day, and pray it at night.

mary.title: Mary in the Bible
mary.sub: 6 studies on the Mother of Jesus
mary.about: Catholics honour Mary because of who she is in the Gospels: the first disciple, who heard God's word and kept it. These studies follow her from the Visitation to the Cross, the upper room and the book of Revelation. The Annunciation and the wedding at Cana are in My RCIA road.

days.title: The Visitation and the Magnificat
days.intro: Mary hurries to visit Elizabeth, and sings her great song of praise.
days.understand: Mary has just said yes to God, and the first thing she does is go to help someone else. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, calls her "the mother of my Lord" and blesses her for believing. Mary's song, the Magnificat, praises a God who lifts up the lowly. The Church sings it every evening.
questions: Mary carries Jesus to Elizabeth. How can you carry Jesus to someone this week?
Elizabeth blesses Mary for believing. What promise of God do you find hard to believe?
Which line of the Magnificat do you want to make your own?
days.live: Pray the Magnificat one evening this week, and visit or call someone who needs company.

days.title: Jesus is presented in the Temple
days.intro: Mary and Joseph bring the baby Jesus to the Temple, where Simeon and Anna recognize him.
days.understand: Mary and Joseph keep the Law as a poor family, offering two birds. Simeon takes Jesus in his arms and calls him a light for the nations. Then he tells Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul: her love for her Son will include suffering. Anna, a widow who prayed for decades, is the first to speak about him to everyone.
questions: Simeon waited his whole life to see God's promise. What are you waiting for?
What does it mean to you that Jesus is "a light for the nations"?
How did Mary live the "sword" Simeon spoke of?
days.live: On 2 February, the Presentation of the Lord, or any day this week, light a candle and pray Simeon's prayer.

days.title: Lost and found in the Temple
days.intro: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and Mary and Joseph search for him for three days.
days.understand: This is the only story of Jesus' childhood after his infancy. Mary and Joseph search in anguish, and find him in his Father's house. Jesus' first recorded words are about his Father. Mary does not understand everything, but she keeps it all in her heart. Faith does not mean having every answer.
questions: Have you ever felt that you lost Jesus? How did you find him again?
Mary did not understand, but she kept these things in her heart. What are you pondering right now?
Jesus went home and was obedient. What does that say about ordinary family life?
days.live: If you feel far from Jesus, go and look for him this week in a church, before the tabernacle.

days.title: Behold your mother
days.intro: From the cross, Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple, and the disciple to her.
days.understand: Mary stands by the cross when most have run away. In one of his last acts, Jesus gives her to John, and John to her. The Church sees each of us in the beloved disciple: Mary is given to us as our mother, and we are invited to take her into our home. Her role is always to lead us to her Son.
questions: What does it mean to you to stand by someone in their suffering?
How do you feel about Mary being given to you as a mother?
What would it look like to "take her into your home"?
days.live: Pray one decade of the Sorrowful Mysteries this week, staying with Mary at the cross.

days.title: Praying with the apostles
days.intro: After the Ascension, the apostles gather in the upper room to pray, with Mary the mother of Jesus.
days.understand: Before the Holy Spirit comes at Pentecost, the first Church is a small community at prayer, and Mary is there among them. She who received the Spirit at the Annunciation now prays for the Spirit to come on the Church. Mary still prays with the Church and for it.
questions: Who do you pray with? Who could you invite to pray with you?
Why do you think Luke mentions Mary by name here?
What do you want to ask the Holy Spirit for?
days.live: Ask Mary this week to pray with you for one person who does not yet know Jesus.

days.title: A woman clothed with the sun
days.intro: John sees a great sign in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, giving birth to a child who will rule the nations.
days.understand: This vision has more than one meaning. The woman is God's people, Israel and the Church, who bring Christ into the world and suffer for it. The Church has also always seen Mary here, the mother of the Messiah, crowned in glory. Mary is a sign of what God wants for the whole Church: to share fully in Christ's victory.
questions: What do you notice about the woman and the dragon in this vision?
How is the Church like a mother?
What hope does this passage give you about the end of the story?
days.live: Pray the Fifth Glorious Mystery, the Coronation of Mary, this week, and ask her to pray for the whole Church.

sacraments.title: The sacraments in the Bible
sacraments.about: The seven sacraments are not inventions of the Church. Each one is rooted in what Jesus did and what the apostles did after him. Read where each sacrament comes from in Scripture, and how the Church celebrates it today.

days.title: Baptism: dying and rising with Christ
days.intro: Paul explains that in Baptism we are buried with Christ and raised to a new life.
days.understand: In the early Church, Baptism was often by going down into the water and coming up again, a picture of burial and resurrection. Paul says something really happens: the old self dies and a new life begins, joined to Christ. Baptism is the door to all the other sacraments. At the Easter Vigil, the elect are baptized and this passage comes alive.
questions: What would you like to leave behind in the waters of Baptism?
Paul says we should consider ourselves "dead to sin and alive to God." What would that change for you?
If you are baptized, what do you know about your Baptism day?
days.live: Bless yourself with holy water when you enter church this week, and remember what Baptism means.

days.title: Confirmation: the gift of the Spirit
days.intro: Peter and John go to Samaria and lay hands on the newly baptized, who receive the Holy Spirit.
days.understand: The Samaritans have been baptized, but the apostles come to complete it by laying hands on them for the gift of the Spirit. The Church sees here the origin of Confirmation. Today the bishop, or a priest he sends, anoints the forehead with chrism and says, "Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit." It strengthens us to live and witness to our faith.
questions: Why do you think the apostles came in person?
Where in your life do you need the strength of the Holy Spirit?
If you are choosing a Confirmation saint, why that saint?
days.live: Pray "Come, Holy Spirit" every morning this week, and ask for one of the seven gifts.

days.title: The Eucharist: this is my body
days.intro: Paul hands on what he received: the words of Jesus at the Last Supper, and how to receive worthily.
days.understand: This is the oldest written account of the Last Supper, written about twenty-five years after it. Paul repeats the words the priest still says at every Mass. He also warns that whoever receives without recognizing the body of the Lord eats unworthily, which is why we prepare, and go to Confession first if we are aware of a serious sin. The Eucharist is the source and summit of the Christian life.
questions: Paul says he "received" and "handed on" these words. Why does that matter?
How do you prepare to meet Jesus at Mass?
If you cannot receive Communion yet, how can you still unite yourself with Jesus at Mass?
days.live: At Mass this week, listen closely to the words of consecration, and make an act of spiritual communion if you do not yet receive.

days.title: Confession: peace be with you
days.intro: On Easter evening, the risen Jesus breathes on the apostles and gives them power to forgive sins.
days.understand: The first gift of the risen Jesus is peace, and the second is the power to forgive. He breathes on the apostles, just as God breathed life into Adam, and sends them to forgive in his name. This is the origin of the sacrament of Penance, also called Reconciliation or Confession. The priest acts in the person of Christ, and what is said there stays there.
questions: Why do you think Jesus' first word to his frightened friends is "Peace"?
What feelings come up when you think about Confession?
Why would Jesus want forgiveness to be spoken aloud by a person?
days.live: Look at the Confession guide in Heartward this week, and find the Confession times at your parish.

days.title: Anointing of the Sick
days.intro: James tells anyone who is sick to call the presbyters of the Church to pray over them and anoint them with oil.
days.understand: James gives very practical advice: pray when you suffer, sing when you are glad, and when you are sick, call the priests. The Church recognizes here the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick. It is not only for the dying; it is for anyone seriously ill or weakened by age, and before serious surgery. It brings strength, peace and courage, and sometimes healing of the body.
questions: Who do you know who is sick and needs prayer?
Why does it matter that the Church prays with the sick, and not only for them?
James joins healing and forgiveness. How are they connected?
days.live: Visit, call or write to someone who is sick this week, and pray for them by name.

days.title: Marriage: a great mystery
days.intro: Paul calls husbands and wives to be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ, and compares marriage to Christ and the Church.
days.understand: This passage begins with mutual submission: "Be subject to one another." Husbands are asked to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, by giving up his life for her. This is not domination; it is self-gift on both sides. Paul calls marriage a great mystery, a living sign of Christ's love for his Church. That is why marriage between the baptized is a sacrament.
questions: What does "be subject to one another" mean in a loving relationship?
How is Christ's love for the Church a model for any love?
What marriages have shown you something of God's love?
days.live: Pray this week for a married couple you know, and for your own vocation.

days.title: Holy Orders: Christ the high priest
days.intro: Hebrews explains what a priest is, and shows that Jesus is the great high priest.
days.understand: A priest is chosen from among the people to offer gifts and sacrifices to God for them. Jesus did not take this honour for himself; the Father gave it to him. He learned obedience through suffering and became the source of salvation. There is only one priest, Christ, and bishops, priests and deacons share in his ministry through the sacrament of Holy Orders.
questions: What do you notice about how Jesus became our high priest?
How has a priest or deacon helped you on your journey?
What does it mean that Jesus can "sympathize with our weakness"?
days.live: Pray for your parish priest by name this week, and if you can, thank him.

virtue.title: Growing in virtue
virtue.about: Virtue is a habit of doing good, and grace makes it grow. These passages look at humility, forgiveness, trust, hope, generosity, strength in weakness and the words we speak. Pick one virtue to practise each week.

days.title: Humility: the mind of Christ
days.intro: Paul asks the Philippians to have the same mind as Christ, who emptied himself and became obedient to death on a cross.
days.understand: This passage is probably an early Christian hymn. It tells the whole story of Jesus in a few lines: he was God, he did not cling to it, he became a servant, he died, and God raised him up. Humility is not thinking badly of ourselves; it is thinking of others, the way Jesus did.
questions: Where do you find it hard to put others first?
What does it tell you about God that Jesus "emptied himself"?
Paul says to do nothing from selfishness or conceit. What would help you live that?
days.live: Let someone else go first this week, in a line, a conversation or a decision, and offer it to Jesus.

days.title: Forgiveness: seventy times seven
days.intro: Peter asks how often he must forgive. Jesus answers with the parable of the unforgiving servant.
days.understand: Peter thinks seven times is generous. Jesus says seventy times seven: without limit. The servant forgiven a huge debt will not forgive a tiny one, and that is the tragedy. We are able to forgive because we have been forgiven so much. Forgiving does not mean saying the wrong was fine, and it can take time; it starts with a choice and a prayer.
questions: Is there someone you find it hard to forgive?
How does remembering God's mercy to you change the way you see others?
What is the difference between forgiving and forgetting?
days.live: Pray by name for someone who hurt you, every day this week, and ask God for the grace to forgive.

days.title: Trust: consider the lilies
days.intro: Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about food and clothing, but to seek first the Kingdom of God.
days.understand: Jesus points to birds and wild flowers: God cares for them, and we are worth much more. This is not a call to be careless, but to trust. The Church calls this divine providence: God guides all things with wisdom and love. Worry looks at tomorrow alone; trust looks at today with the Father.
questions: What do you worry about most often?
What would "seek first the Kingdom" look like in your choices this week?
Where have you seen God's care for you in small things?
days.live: Spend five minutes outside this week looking at birds or plants, and hand your worries to the Father.

days.title: Hope: nothing can separate us
days.intro: Paul writes that present sufferings are nothing compared with the glory to come, and nothing can separate us from God's love.
days.understand: Paul does not deny suffering: all creation groans, and so do we. But he looks forward to glory, and he knows the Spirit prays in us when we do not know how. His great list at the end, death, life, angels, powers, nothing, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Hope is trust in that love, reaching into the future.
questions: What suffering are you carrying right now?
Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness when we do not know how to pray. Have you felt that?
Which line of the last verses would you like to remember?
days.live: Write Romans 8:38-39 on a card and keep it where you will see it every day.

days.title: Generosity: a cheerful giver
days.intro: Paul encourages the Corinthians to give to the poor in Jerusalem, because God loves a cheerful giver.
days.understand: Paul is collecting money for poor Christians far away. He does not command a sum; he asks each to give freely, from the heart. Whoever sows generously reaps generously, and God gives us enough so that we can share. Giving to the poor is giving to Christ, and it ends in thanksgiving to God.
questions: What makes it hard or easy for you to give?
Generosity is not only money. What else could you give?
Who in your community is in need right now?
days.live: Give something this week, time, money or help, quietly and cheerfully, to someone in need.

days.title: Strength in weakness
days.intro: Paul prays three times to be freed from a "thorn in the flesh," and hears: "My grace is sufficient for you."
days.understand: We do not know what Paul's thorn was, and perhaps that helps: each of us can put our own weakness there. God does not take it away, but gives grace that is enough. Paul learns to boast of his weakness, because then Christ's power lives in him. When we are weak, then we are strong.
questions: What is your "thorn", a weakness or struggle that does not go away?
Have you ever experienced God's strength when you felt weakest?
What would change if you stopped hiding your weakness from God?
days.live: Offer one weakness or struggle to God each morning this week with the words "Your grace is enough for me."

days.title: Taming the tongue
days.intro: James warns that the tongue is small but powerful: with it we bless God and curse people made in his image.
days.understand: James uses vivid pictures: a bit in a horse's mouth, a ship's rudder, a spark that sets a forest on fire. Words can build up or tear down. The Church warns against gossip, rash judgment and revealing others' faults without need. A Christian's speech should be like fresh water from a clean spring.
questions: When do you find it hardest to control what you say?
Can you remember words that built you up? Words that hurt you?
What would help you stop before speaking?
days.live: Go one whole day this week without saying anything negative about anyone, and notice what changes.

parables.title: The parables of Jesus
parables.sub: 7 studies on the stories Jesus told
parables.about: Jesus taught with stories taken from daily life: seeds, coins, banquets and workers. A parable invites us to take a side and find ourselves in it. The lost sheep and the prodigal son are in My RCIA road; these are seven more.

days.title: The sower and the seed
days.intro: A farmer scatters seed on a path, on rocks, among thorns and on good soil, and Jesus explains what it means.
days.understand: The sower is generous: he throws seed everywhere. The difference is in the soil, in how the word is received. Some hear and forget, some start with joy but give up, some are choked by worries and riches, and some bear fruit, thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. Jesus explains that parables open the mystery of the Kingdom to those willing to listen.
questions: Which kind of soil describes your heart right now?
What "thorns" choke the word in your life?
What helps the word take root in you?
days.live: Choose one line from Sunday's Gospel this week and come back to it each day.

days.title: The Good Samaritan
days.intro: A lawyer asks, "Who is my neighbour?" Jesus answers with a story about a hated foreigner who stops to help.
days.understand: The priest and the Levite pass by, perhaps for religious reasons. The Samaritan, an outsider and an enemy, is the one moved with compassion. Jesus turns the question around: not "who deserves my help?" but "who will I be a neighbour to?" The Church Fathers also saw Jesus himself as the Good Samaritan, who comes to heal wounded humanity.
questions: Who are the people you find it easy to pass by?
When has someone been a Good Samaritan to you?
What stops us from helping, even when we see the need?
days.live: Stop for someone this week whom you would usually pass by.

days.title: The treasure and the pearl
days.intro: A man finds a treasure in a field, a merchant finds a pearl of great price, and both sell everything to have it.
days.understand: These two short parables are about joy. The man does not sell everything grudgingly; he does it "in his joy." The Kingdom of God is worth more than anything we could give up for it. The Church teaches that following Jesus means putting him first, before every good thing we own.
questions: What has been your "treasure in the field" on this journey?
Is there anything you are afraid you might have to give up?
Where do you feel the joy of finding God?
days.live: Write down what you have found on your journey to the Church so far, and thank God for it.

days.title: The talents
days.intro: A master entrusts his servants with different amounts of money and later asks what they did with it.
days.understand: A talent was a huge sum, many years of wages. Two servants use what they received and double it; the third buries it out of fear. The master is not angry that he earned less, but that he did nothing. God gives each of us different gifts, and asks us to use them with courage for others.
questions: What gifts has God given you?
What fear makes you "bury" a gift?
How could you use one of your gifts for your parish or community?
days.live: Use one of your gifts this week for someone else: cooking, listening, a skill, a language.

days.title: The rich fool
days.intro: A man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance. Jesus warns against greed and tells of a rich man who built bigger barns.
days.understand: The rich man talks only to himself: my crops, my barns, my soul. He plans everything except his death. God calls him a fool, not because he is rich, but because he is not rich toward God. Our life does not consist in what we own. The Church calls us to be detached from riches so that our heart is free for God.
questions: What do you tend to store up "just in case"?
What does it mean to be "rich toward God"?
If your life were asked of you tonight, what would matter most?
days.live: Give away something you do not need this week.

days.title: The wedding feast
days.intro: A king prepares a wedding feast for his son. The invited guests refuse, so he invites everyone from the streets.
days.understand: The Kingdom of God is a wedding feast, and everyone is invited, good and bad alike. Those who refuse are too busy with their farms and business. The guest without a wedding garment shows that accepting the invitation also means letting ourselves be changed. Early Christians saw the garment as the white robe of Baptism.
questions: What excuses do people give for not coming to God's feast? What are yours?
How does it feel to know you are invited?
What "wedding garment" is God offering you?
days.live: Invite someone this week to come with you to Mass or to a parish event.

days.title: The workers in the vineyard
days.intro: A landowner hires workers throughout the day, then pays them all the same wage.
days.understand: Those who worked all day feel cheated, and many of us would agree with them. But the landowner has been just to them and generous to the others. God's grace is not a wage we earn; it is a gift. That is good news for anyone who comes to faith late in life: it is never too late to be called into the vineyard.
questions: Do you feel more like the early workers or the late ones?
Why does God's generosity sometimes bother us?
What does it mean to you that it is never too late?
days.live: Thank God this week for calling you, at the hour he chose.

mercy.title: Meeting Jesus: healing and mercy
mercy.sub: 7 studies on people whose lives Jesus changed
mercy.about: In the Gospels, people meet Jesus one by one: the sick, the outsiders, the ashamed and the curious. Each encounter shows who Jesus is and what he wants to do for us. Put yourself in their place as you read.

days.title: Through the roof
days.intro: Four friends lower a paralysed man through a roof to Jesus, who forgives his sins and heals him.
days.understand: The friends cannot get through the crowd, so they dig through the roof. Jesus sees their faith, and his first words are not about the body but about sin. Then he heals the body too, to show he has the power to forgive. The Church continues both works in the sacraments of Penance and Anointing.
questions: Who has carried you to Jesus when you could not go yourself?
Who could you "carry" to Jesus through your prayer?
Why do you think Jesus forgave the man's sins first?
days.live: Pray every day this week for a friend who is struggling, as if carrying them to Jesus.

days.title: The woman who touched his cloak
days.intro: A woman ill for twelve years reaches out in the crowd to touch Jesus' clothes, and is healed.
days.understand: Her illness made her unclean under the Law, so she was cut off from others for twelve years. She hopes to touch Jesus without being noticed. But Jesus stops and looks for her, because he wants to heal more than her body: he calls her "daughter" in front of everyone. In the sacraments, power still goes out from Jesus to those who reach for him in faith.
questions: What have you been carrying for a long time?
Why do you think Jesus wanted to see her face?
How can you reach out to Jesus this week?
days.live: Come a few minutes early to Mass this week and bring Jesus one long-standing need.

days.title: Blind Bartimaeus
days.intro: A blind beggar shouts to Jesus for mercy, and will not be silenced.
days.understand: People tell Bartimaeus to be quiet, but he shouts louder. Jesus stops and asks, "What do you want me to do for you?" Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, perhaps all he owned, and asks to see. Once he can see, he follows Jesus on the way. His cry, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me," is one of the oldest Christian prayers.
questions: If Jesus asked you, "What do you want me to do for you?", what would you say?
Who or what tries to silence your prayer?
What "cloak" might you need to throw off to follow Jesus?
days.live: Answer Jesus' question in writing this week: what do you want him to do for you?

days.title: The woman at the well
days.intro: At noon by a well, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, and offers her living water.
days.understand: She comes at the hottest hour, perhaps to avoid other people. Jesus breaks every barrier: he is a Jewish man talking alone with a Samaritan woman. He knows her whole story and does not reject her. The Church sees God's thirst here: God thirsts for us, so that we may thirst for him. She runs back to town to tell everyone, the first missionary to the Samaritans. This Gospel is read on the Third Sunday of Lent for the first scrutiny of the elect.
questions: What are you thirsty for?
How does it feel that Jesus knows everything about you and still seeks you?
Who could you tell about what Jesus has done for you?
days.live: Each time you drink water this week, say a short prayer: "Jesus, give me living water."

days.title: Zacchaeus
days.intro: A rich, disliked tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus, and Jesus invites himself to his house.
days.understand: Zacchaeus is curious, small and unpopular. Jesus stops under the tree, calls him by name, and says, "Today I must stay at your house." Before any change, Jesus offers friendship. Then Zacchaeus changes on his own: he gives half to the poor and repays fourfold. The Church cites him as an example of making amends. The Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.
questions: What "tree" have you climbed to see Jesus?
Jesus called Zacchaeus by name. How does it feel that he knows yours?
Is there anything you need to make right with someone?
days.live: If you owe someone an apology or a debt, take one step to make it right this week.

days.title: Neither do I condemn you
days.intro: Religious leaders bring a woman caught in adultery to Jesus to test him. He writes on the ground and says, "Let the one without sin throw the first stone."
days.understand: The leaders use the woman as a trap. Jesus refuses to be part of it, and one by one, from the oldest, they leave. Then Jesus is alone with her, and he is the only one without sin who could condemn her. He does not. But he also says, "Go, and sin no more." Mercy does not call sin good; it frees us to begin again.
questions: Have you ever been quick to judge someone?
How does Jesus hold together mercy and truth here?
What would "go and sin no more" mean for you?
days.live: Before you judge someone this week, stop and pray for them instead.

days.title: The one who came back
days.intro: Jesus heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him.
days.understand: All ten are healed on the way, but only one turns back, praising God aloud, and falls at Jesus' feet. Jesus asks where the other nine are. Gratitude completes the healing: to the one who returned he says, "Your faith has saved you." The word Eucharist means thanksgiving; every Mass is our turning back to say thank you.
questions: What has God done for you that you have not yet thanked him for?
Why do you think the other nine did not come back?
How does gratitude change the way you see your life?
days.live: Write down three things you are thankful for each night this week.
